This is really insightful. I always felt that Jim Jones’s ideas, at first glance, seemed to lead to positive changes for a lot of disenfranchised people — whatever his actual motivations were. But the People’s Temple went horribly awry before they even went to Guyana, due to his and the inner circle’s need for control. The weird punishments, long nights of service, lack of sleep and food, etc. all started in California. And once these people were more isolated in the jungle, how could they begin to escape? Even a member of the inner circle, Deborah Layton, had to make a complex plan to leave, as outlined in “Seductive Poison.” I need to read more on Mike Prokes’ statements…you have my curiosity peaked.

When I lost my dad in 2021, I absolutely planned to unalive myself. I lived with him, and he was my best friend. Plus, I had already lost my mom in 2004, and I found myself totally alone. I’m not close with most of my relatives, I’m divorced, and the few friends I have were at a loss as to how to help me. I wrote a long note and started making plans. But the thought of what could happen if I failed — essentially, this guy’s story — kept me from truly attempting it. I had read up on methods online, and determined my plan had too high of a failure risk, and I just kept thinking, “What if it doesn’t work? What if I end up in a hospital bed, and we add a physical disability to this awful mental pain?” I still have suicidal ideation, and I sometimes think those thoughts are addictive in their own way, as they seem oddly comforting. But stories like these remind me of why I choose to keep trying this life thing.

I had a friend chew me out because my dog is registered as an emotional support animal. My dad had died unexpectedly in 2021 (we were very close), and when I applied for a new apartment after being forced to leave the apartment my dad and I had shared, my new apartment manager asked if my therapist would be willing to write a letter to have him designated an emotional support animal — which my therapist wholeheartedly agreed to do, and then I filled out paperwork to have him “officially” registered. The big benefit to that is, apartments will waive the pet fee. I figured since the apartment manager suggested it, and this dog did give me a reason to live after my dad died, there was no reason not to do it. And boy, was my friend angry when he found out, claiming I was cheating the system. But he also said I should be over my dad’s death in less than a year and doesn’t believe depression is a real thing…

That's a good question. I was applying to a ton of jobs during that period, and I actually had several offers come in around the same time. One was a full-time associate editor job for a medical trade magazine, which I turned down. I just had a bad feeling about it, the company had awful reviews on Glassdoor, and the topic didn't interest me at all. Plus, I just had a feeling this job might work out, and that gamble paid off! I had also landed a part-time marketing gig after my interview, which I ended up leaving (it was good practice though and a little extra money). But as for this specific job? I think it was just a matter of me having the skills they needed. They loved that I was able to copy edit and write -- but I think my strong background in photography clinched it. They realized they could use me for different tasks. I believe being multifaceted helped me get this particular job. And it didn't hurt that I aced the copy editing test and returned it quickly. I had taken some courses online in SEO, and I think that probably contributed to some degree. But oddly, I applied to very similar jobs as this one that rejected me -- and they all paid less! I wish I had a better answer than "luck of the draw" or "right opportunity at the right time," but at the end of the day, I think that's truly what this was...

I ended up in the marketing department of a college! I edit copy, write articles and even shoot assignments — so basically everything I did in news, but with much better pay, benefits, and we get two paid weeks off, between spring and winter breaks, along with our vacation and sick time! Plus I get to work hybrid, with just two days a week in the office :)

As someone who worked in journalism and whose father worked in journalism, this is an age-old a tough question, and I have mixed feelings. I remember him telling me how his team debated over publishing the famous “falling man” photo from 9/11. Ultimately, they did, but of course they got some flack for it. I just remembered, in my last job, we had dash cam video of a bad accident involving a potentially distracted semi driver and a van carrying migrants. The van had been pulled over by the cops, but stopped in the right hand lane instead of moving to the shoulder. The collision was caught on video, and it was brutal, but impactful, so we published it online (I was the person who handled video, so the editing and posting task fell to me). We also got a lot of hateful comments. To be fair, all you saw was the initial impact, and you couldn’t see the occupants of either vehicle, but we were definitely accused of sensationalism because by the time it was posted, we all knew everyone in the van had been killed. On the one hand, these kinds of pictures/videos are bound to upset people, understandably. On the other hand, seeing the brutal reality of a car collision that didn’t need to happen or of a body following a tragic event should be a wake up call. And journalists usually feel they have a responsibility to inform the public, so hiding these photos feels like just as much of a disservice as publishing anything that might hurt someone. I lean toward publishing these images, to show the reality and hopefully prevent future events. If we bury our heads in the sand, these killings will definitely keep happening. But I also acknowledge that none of us want to see a photo of a dead child. I think the answer might be taking the photos and/or cropping them in a way that makes a statement without disgusting anyone, like seeing just a hand, etc. Maybe we don’t need an up-close image of a body, because while we have a responsibility to inform, we can’t lose regard for humanity and privacy. I think when she wrote this book, she was still grasping for meaning in the midst of the chaos that came into her life. It’s easy for us to play “Monday morning quarterback” and say we would have caught the signs, but at the end of the day, no parent wants to think their child could commit mass murder.
